verses.note: The same God who is Elohim, creator of everything, is now called by his personal covenant name. The pairing tells the reader that the maker of the cosmos and the God who later bound himself to Israel are one and the same.

God names humanity as he named day, night, sky, land, and seas in chapter 1. Naming expresses his authority over what he has made, and human beings, for all their rule over the animals, receive their own name from him.

The verse joins two names: El Elyon, a title a Canaanite priest-king could use, and the LORD, the personal name of Abram's God. Abram does not reject the title; he claims it for the LORD, declaring that the Most High is not an unknown deity but the God who made promises to him.
Most divine names in Genesis are given by God or used in worship by the patriarchs. This one is given by an Egyptian slave out of her own encounter, and Scripture keeps it.
El Shaddai becomes the name of blessing and fruitfulness in Genesis (28:3, 35:11, 48:3, 49:25). The name is given here, at the point where only the power of God can make the promise come true.
El Olam joins El Elyon (Genesis 14:19), El Roi (16:13), and El Shaddai (17:1) among the names by which the patriarchs knew God, each drawn from an experience of him.

El was the common Semitic word for God and also the name of the high god in Canaanite religion. By naming the altar El Elohe Israel Jacob claims that El is no distant deity of the region but the God who met and renamed him.

El Shaddai is the name tied to the patriarchs' promises of offspring (17:1, 28:3, 48:3). Exodus 6:3 says God was known to the fathers by this name, which frames the patriarchal period as a time of promise awaiting the fuller self-revelation of the exodus.
El Shaddai in Genesis is the name of God attached to fruitfulness and promise. Invoking it here, Jacob appeals to God's own commitment to the family, not to his sons' cleverness.

El Shaddai is tied in Genesis to the promise of fruitfulness (17:1-2, 28:3, 35:11). Jacob's use of the name here, before adopting two boys, fits that pattern: the God who makes a barren family fruitful is the one he invokes.

Jacob gathers names for God in a single line: the Mighty One of Jacob, the Shepherd (compare 48:15), and the Stone or Rock of Israel. Each names God by what he has been to Jacob: strength, care, and a sure foundation, possibly with a memory of the stone at Bethel (28:18-22).

God gives his name, but in a form that explains rather than labels him: he is the one who is, and the one who will be with his people. The name makes relationship possible without making God manageable.

The personal name joins God's being to his history with a family: YHWH is ‘the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’. God is known not in the abstract but through what he has promised and done.

El Shaddai was the name tied to promises of offspring and land (Genesis 17:1; 28:3; 35:11). The name YHWH will now be tied to redemption, so that every later use of it recalls the God who brought Israel out of Egypt (20:2).
God identifies himself by his personal name, YHWH, revealed to Moses at the bush (3:14-15), and by an event: the one who brought Israel out. The name and the history interpret each other.

God's name stands for God himself as he has made himself known. To use it to back a lie, to manipulate, or to cover one's own purposes treats God as a tool. The command protects the name because it protects the God who gave it.

When God proclaims his name, he explains it. The name YHWH, first given at the bush (3:14-15), is now unfolded as a description of his character in verses 6 and 7. In Scripture God's name is his revealed identity, not a label.

‘The Holy One’ is Isaiah's characteristic way of naming God, usually as ‘the Holy One of Israel’, about twenty-five times in the book. Holiness here means incomparability: there is no one to set beside him.

God's name is his revealed reputation. When his people are defeated, the nations conclude that their God is powerless, and his name is reviled. Ezekiel 36:20-23 gives the same reason for the return: God acts for the sake of his holy name.
God's ‘name’ is his revealed character and reputation. The first petition asks that God make himself known as holy, which is why it comes before any request for bread.

The words egō eimi recall the name God gives himself in Isaiah. Here they are chiefly messianic, but John lets the reader hear an overtone that will become explicit in 8:58, where ‘before Abraham was born, I am’ draws an attempt to stone him.

On the lake Jesus does what the Old Testament reserves for God and speaks in words that echo God's name for himself. This is the first of John's egō eimi sayings, set in a scene of rescue, so that the divine name is heard first as comfort: the one who treads the sea is the one who comes to his frightened people.
The absolute ‘I am’ takes up the form in which Israel's God declared his uniqueness. Faith here is not assent to a doctrine about Jesus but belief that he is who God is.

Jesus speaks of himself in the form Israel's Scriptures reserve for God's own being. The verse is one of the texts on which the Council of Nicaea's confession (325), that the Son is eternal and of one being with the Father, rested.
Jesus applies to himself the self-designation by which the LORD in Isaiah distinguishes himself from idols. The betrayal, which might seem to disprove his claims, is turned into evidence for them.

To reveal God's name is to make God himself known as he is. At the burning bush and on Sinai God proclaimed his name to Moses (Exodus 3:14-15, 34:5-7), and Isaiah promised a day when his people would know his name (Isaiah 52:6). Jesus claims to have done what those passages promised: the Father's name, his character and presence, has been made known in the Son.

The words by which Israel's God names himself in Isaiah, ‘I am He’, are spoken by Jesus at the moment of his arrest, and armed men fall before them. John presents the one being arrested as the bearer of the divine name (17:6, 17:11), who nonetheless lets himself be taken.
God's name is his reputation among the nations. The people who bear his name can bring it honor or contempt, which is why the first petition of the Lord's Prayer asks that it be hallowed.
